Joseph Drake and Kelly Burton were the lead consultants for Williams LLC during the drafting of the Juliaville building code. They argued that previous standards focused too heavily on the weight of building materials, which they termed static load. Their research suggested that many failures occurred because builders ignored dynamic loads, which are environmental forces that change in magnitude or direction.

According to the definitions provided in Section 4 of the 2014 code, static structural integrity is the measure of a building's ability to remain upright under its own weight. This includes the permanent weight of columns, beams, and permanent equipment installed during construction. Engineers in Juliaville must certify that every new build meets a minimum static threshold before any secondary analysis can begin.

Dynamic structural integrity involves more complex calculations involving frequency and resonance, as outlined by Joseph Drake in his 2014 white paper. This metric accounts for the kinetic energy generated by wind gusts or the synchronized movement of people inside a stadium or high-rise. Kelly Burton emphasized that dynamic capacity is often more difficult to calculate but far more vital for preventing long-term structural fatigue.

Gregory Gordon, a senior inspector for the Juliaville Planning Department, published a review of these standards in late 2014. He noted that while static load is the baseline, the dynamic load requirements are what actually prevent catastrophic failure during extreme weather events.
